title: Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger
paragraphs: In 1916, Albert Einstein said that space could have waves. He had set down his rules for gravity the year before. That was a new way to think about gravity. It said that space could change shape. The waves move as fast as light. They stretch and squeeze space from side to side. You can think of a wave in a pond. But these waves are not in water. They pass through space itself. The space gets a bit wider, then a bit narrower. A change in how mass is spread out can make them. The waves can go far from the place where they start. They carry news of what made them. Einstein knew the waves would be very small. But were they real? For years, people did not agree. At the time, no one had seen them. It was hard to tell what such small waves could do. The debate went on till a meeting at Chapel Hill in 1957.

In 1916, Albert Einstein predicted that waves could travel through space. He did this a year after finishing his equations for gravity. His work offered a new way to think about gravity and space. The waves stretch and squeeze space sideways as they travel at the speed of light. This does not mean a wave in water. It means that space itself changes shape as the wave passes. As a wave passes, the distance between objects can change a little. They can be made when the way a source’s mass is spread out changes over time. The waves can travel far from the place where they are made. Einstein knew the waves would be very small. The stretching and squeezing are very slight, even close to the source. Such small changes are hard to notice. For many years, scientists argued about whether the waves were real. The debate went on until a meeting at Chapel Hill in 1957.

In 1916, Albert Einstein predicted gravitational waves. A year earlier, he had completed the equations of general relativity, his theory of gravity. The full equations describe how matter and energy affect the shape of spacetime. He found that simpler equations allowed waves in weak fields of gravity. This approach made the equations easier to solve by treating gravity as a weak field. The waves travel at the speed of light and stretch and squeeze space sideways. As a wave passes, distances across its path change slightly, then change back. They arise when the way mass is spread in a source changes in a particular way over time. This change must have the right pattern; not every change in mass distribution makes these waves. Einstein knew the waves would be very small. The waves carry information away from their source, though their effects are hard to detect. Scientists debated whether they were real until the Chapel Hill conference in 1957.

In 1916, a year after completing the field equations of general relativity, Albert Einstein predicted gravitational waves. Using a linear approximation for weak fields, he found solutions that travel at the speed of light. In this approximation, the departure from flat spacetime is small, so terms beyond the first order can be neglected. The approximation applies where the gravitational field is sufficiently weak for those higher-order terms to be small. These waves stretch and squeeze space at right angles to their direction of travel. The resulting strain describes fractional changes in distance. They arise from changes in a source’s mass quadrupole moment, a measure of how its mass is distributed. Not every change in a mass distribution produces such radiation; the change must affect its quadrupole moment. Einstein knew their amplitudes would be tiny. That made their detection a major challenge. Until the Chapel Hill conference in 1957, scientists debated whether the waves were physically real.

He found that the linearized equations for weak gravitational fields admit transverse waves of spatial strain, which travel at the speed of light. The linear approximation treats deviations from flat spacetime as small, retaining only terms of first order in the metric perturbation. The approximation applies in a regime where the perturbation and the neglected nonlinear terms are sufficiently small. The strain describes fractional changes in separation transverse to propagation. These waves arise from changes in the source’s mass quadrupole moment, which describes an aspect of its mass distribution. A changing mass distribution does not necessarily radiate: the quadrupole moment must vary in the relevant way. The small predicted strain made experimental detection exceptionally challenging. Einstein knew the waves would have remarkably small amplitudes, and their physical reality was debated until the Chapel Hill conference in 1957.

In 1916, the year after the final formulation of the field equations of general relativity, Albert Einstein predicted gravitational waves. He found that the linearized weak-field equations had wave solutions: transverse waves of spatial strain that travel at the speed of light, generated by time variations of the mass quadrupole moment of the source. In this perturbative treatment, the metric is expanded about flat spacetime, with nonlinear contributions discarded, and the resulting transverse strain represents fractional changes in the separation of freely falling test masses. The weak-field approximation permits superposition of these perturbations, although it does not capture their full nonlinear dynamics. For an isolated, slowly moving source, the leading far-field strain is proportional to the transverse-traceless projection of the quadrupole moment’s second time derivative, evaluated at retarded time. Einstein understood that gravitational-wave amplitudes would be remarkably small. Until the Chapel Hill conference in 1957, there was significant debate about the physical reality of gravitational waves.

In 1916, Schwarzschild found a new way to use Einstein’s rules. The rules tell us how things pull on each other. His work would help us learn about black holes. A black hole is a place in space. Its pull is so strong that not even light can get out. In 1963, Kerr built on this work for black holes that spin. They spin like a top. His work was a piece of a big puzzle. It took a long time to put more pieces in place. Later, more work helped us work out what happens when two black holes join. They can move round each other first. Two black holes can get close and pull on each other. As they get close, they move faster. At last, they join and make one black hole. We can now tell what waves that crash makes. Before this, no one had seen two black holes join.

Hulse and Taylor found two stars. The stars go round each other. One sends out signals, like ticks from a clock. Later, Taylor and Weisberg saw the stars lose energy. This showed that waves in space are real. The two stars are far away. They pull on each other as they move. The waves take energy away from the stars. That is why the stars lose energy. The pull of each star helps keep the other in its path. As the stars lose energy, their paths change too. By timing the ticks, people can learn how the stars move. The waves are too faint for us to see with our eyes. Then scientists saw that they could learn more. They could look for the waves themselves. They could see how big the waves are and how they rise and fall. This could help them learn more about space and test ideas about gravity.

Hulse and Taylor found a pair of stars that orbit each other. One is a pulsar, a star that sends out steady pulses. Later, Taylor and Weisberg saw that the pair was losing energy. This showed that gravitational waves, or waves in space, are real. As they orbit, the stars pull on each other. The waves carry energy away from their motion. That loss gives clues about the waves, even without detecting them directly. The pulses act like a clock that helps scientists track the stars as they move. As energy leaves the system, the orbit changes. The rate of that change can be compared with what the theory says should happen. Scientists then saw a way to learn more. They could detect the waves directly and measure their size and how they rise and fall. This could help them study other star pairs and test Einstein’s theory where gravity is strong and changing.

Hulse and Taylor discovered a binary pulsar: two stars that orbit each other. One star sends out regular pulses, like ticks from a clock. Later, Taylor and Weisberg saw that the system was losing energy. This showed that gravitational waves exist, and scientists then saw that direct measurements of these waves could tell them more. The energy loss matched what the theory predicted for waves carrying energy away from the orbit. This was indirect evidence, rather than a direct detection of the waves. The timing of the pulses lets researchers track changes in the orbit. The measured loss of energy was a powerful test of the prediction, but it did not give a direct record of the waves passing through a detector. Their strength and phase, or place in a wave’s cycle, could help scientists study other systems. They could also test Einstein’s theory of gravity where fields are strong and changing.

A century after the fundamental predictions of Einstein and Schwarzschild, we report the first direct detection of gravitational waves. We also report the first direct observation of a binary black hole system merging to form a single black hole. Our observations provide unique access to the properties of space-time in the strong-field, high-velocity regime. They confirm predictions of general relativity for the nonlinear dynamics of highly disturbed black holes. In this regime, the gravitational field cannot be treated as a small perturbation. The emitted waves encode information about the merger and the evolution of the resulting black hole, making the signal a probe of gravity and space-time dynamics under these extreme conditions. The observed waveform therefore enables comparisons with relativistic predictions for the evolution of a binary in the strong-field regime. This allows us to test general relativity in a dynamical setting where strong gravity and rapid motion both shape the signal.

Two black holes may have made the wave we saw. A black hole is a place in space with a pull so strong that even light cannot get out. They went round each other and drew close. The waves spread out through space. As the holes got near, they went round each other faster. Then they joined into one black hole. The new hole shook and grew still. It shook for a short time, much like a bell after it is struck. In the end, just one hole was left. As the holes drew close, waves took energy away. The wave grew stronger and faster in one fifth of a second. It went through about eight cycles. Each cycle was one rise and fall of the wave. Its rate rose from 35 to 150 cycles per second, where it was strongest. Its early rise tells us about the mass of the two holes.

To reach an orbital frequency of 75 Hz, half the gravitational-wave frequency, the objects must have been extremely compact and close together; in a Newtonian approximation, equal point masses orbiting at this frequency would be only $\simeq 350$ km apart. Scientists use tools far apart to find waves in space. The waves make space stretch and squeeze as they pass. The tools are in two places. A real wave can reach both places. Noise near one tool may not reach the other. This helps them tell a real wave from noise close to a tool. It also helps them find where the wave came from. The tools can also help tell which way the wave stretches space. Each LIGO tool has two long arms that meet at a right angle. Each arm is a long way from end to end. That is four kilometers, or about two and a half miles. Each arm has a mirror at each end. A wave makes the arms change length by different amounts. The change can make one arm grow and the other shrink. Light goes down each arm and comes back. The light bounces off the mirrors before it comes back. The tool reads changes in the light to tell how strong the wave is.

Gravitational-wave detectors far apart help scientists tell real signals from local noise and find where the waves came from. Gravitational-wave detectors at widely separated sites help scientists distinguish waves from local instrumental and environmental noise, locate sources, and measure wave polarization. Comparing signals at different sites helps separate a passing wave from disturbances at just one location. Polarization describes the pattern of stretching and squeezing produced by a wave as it passes. Each LIGO detector is an interferometer, a device that compares light from two arms. The arms meet at right angles and are each four kilometers long, with a mirror at each end. The mirrors act as test masses whose positions are used to measure the length changes. A passing wave changes their lengths by different amounts, shifting the phase, or timing, of the light that returns from each arm. The comparison is sensitive to the difference between the two arm lengths, not simply to a change in one arm. The detector reads this shift to measure the wave’s strain. Strain describes the size of this change relative to the arm length.

Widely separated detectors distinguish gravitational waves from local noise, locate sources, and measure wave polarizations. The network enables source localization by comparing signals recorded at different sites. The same network also constrains the polarization content of the signal, since differently oriented detectors respond differently to an incident wave. Each Advanced LIGO detector is a modified Michelson interferometer. It has two 4 km arms at right angles, with mirrors that act as test masses. Each arm is bounded by two mirrors, whose positions provide the reference for its length measurement. A passing wave produces a differential length change, $\Delta L(t) = \delta L_x - \delta L_y = h(t)L$, where $h$ is the strain projected onto the detector. The projected strain depends on the direction and polarization of the wave relative to the detector. This change shifts the phase difference between returning light fields, yielding an optical signal proportional to strain at the output photodetector. The output therefore encodes the differential response of the interferometer to an incident wave.

To measure gravitational waves, the detectors add several features to a basic Michelson interferometer. In each arm, two mirrors form a resonant optical cavity, where light reflects back and forth, multiplying the wave’s effect on the light’s phase by a factor of 300. The phase describes where a light wave is in its cycle. The light’s repeated trips through the arm allow a passing wave to produce a larger cumulative change in its phase. A partially transmissive mirror at the input builds up laser power throughout the detector. The input mirror reflects some light back into the interferometer while allowing some to pass through. Another such mirror at the output broadens the range of signal frequencies the cavities can detect. Similarly, the output mirror reflects part of the light and transmits the rest. The laser is stabilized in amplitude, frequency, and beam shape. At the output, a technique called homodyne readout extracts the gravitational-wave signal from the light.

To measure gravitational waves with sufficient sensitivity, the detectors enhance the basic Michelson interferometer. Each arm contains a resonant optical cavity formed by two test mass mirrors. Light makes repeated passes between the mirrors, multiplying the wave’s effect on its phase by a factor of 300 without requiring physically longer interferometer arms. At the input, a partially transmissive power-recycling mirror increases laser power through resonant buildup in the interferometer. This raises 20 W of laser input to 700 W incident on the beam splitter, with 100 kW circulating in each arm cavity. At the output, a partially transmissive signal-recycling mirror broadens the arm cavities’ bandwidth. This improves extraction of the gravitational-wave signal across a wider range of frequencies. A 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser illuminates the interferometer and is stabilized in amplitude, frequency, and beam geometry. The signal is extracted from the light at the output port using a homodyne readout.

To measure gravitational waves with sufficient sensitivity, the detectors enhance the basic Michelson interferometer. Each arm contains a resonant optical cavity, formed by two test mass mirrors, that multiplies the wave’s effect on the light phase by a factor of 300. A partially transmissive power-recycling mirror at the input provides resonant buildup of laser light: 20 W input becomes 700 W incident on the beam splitter and 100 kW circulating in each arm cavity. At the output, a partially transmissive signal-recycling mirror optimizes signal extraction by broadening the arm cavities’ bandwidth. In both recycling configurations, partial transmission permits light to enter or leave while the remaining light is reflected. These enhancements increase the observable phase response while also improving the efficiency with which the interferometer extracts signals over a wider frequency range. A 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser, stabilized in amplitude, frequency, and beam geometry, illuminates the interferometer. Homodyne readout extracts the gravitational-wave signal at the output port.

Each site has tools to watch for things that can throw the detectors off. Some track shakes in the ground. A truck can make the ground shake as it goes by. Some track sound, radio waves, weather, and power lines. A loud noise can be picked up too. Wind and rain can make noise at a site. These tools help us see if a shake or a sound may change the data. The tools keep track of what is going on near the detectors. Then we can look at the tool data and the detector data at the same time. Other data show how the detectors and their controls work. We use GPS time to line up all the data. This time comes from space. The data line up within ten millionths of a second. At each site, we check the time with a special clock. We also use a second GPS tool.

New LIGO tools can sense much smaller waves in space than the first ones could. A wave can be too weak for an old tool to sense. A new one can pick up some of these weak waves. In their best range, they are three to five times as good. For some slower waves, they are more than ten times as good. This lets LIGO reach farther. The waves get weak as they go far. It can search much more of space. If it can sense waves half as strong, it can search eight times as much nearby space. For black hole pairs like GW150914, this search covered ten times as much space over time as past searches. How long the search lasts also helps set how many pairs it might find. The new tools still cannot find every pair. Some pairs are too far away for their waves to be picked up.

LIGO detectors pick up waves that stretch and squeeze space. In their best range, from 100 to 300 waves per second, they are three to five times as sensitive as the first ones. The number of waves per second tells us how fast a wave goes through its cycle. Below 60 waves per second, they are more than ten times as sensitive. A more sensitive detector can pick up a weaker wave. This lets them search farther. The waves get weaker as they travel farther from their source. That means the new detectors can find some sources that were too far away for the first ones. If their reach doubles, they can search eight times as much nearby space. For black hole pairs with masses like GW150914, this search covered ten times as much space over time as past searches. The length of the search also affects how many pairs it might find.

Current LIGO detectors can measure much smaller strains, or stretches and squeezes of space, than the first LIGO detectors could. In their most sensitive range, from 100 to 300 cycles per second, they are three to five times as sensitive. Frequency tells us how many wave cycles pass a point each second. Below 60 cycles per second, they are more than ten times as sensitive. A more sensitive detector can pick up weaker waves from a given kind of source. The waves grow weaker as they travel farther from their source. The farther the detector can see, the larger the region it can search for such events. For nearby sources, doubling sensitivity lets LIGO search eight times as much space. For black hole pairs with masses like GW150914, this search covered about ten times the space-time volume of earlier searches. How long the detectors observe also helps determine the space-time volume searched.

In their most sensitive frequency band, from 100 to 300 Hz, current LIGO detectors are three to five times more sensitive to strain than the first LIGO detectors. Strain is the stretching and squeezing of space caused by a passing gravitational wave. Below 60 Hz, the gain is even greater: the detectors are more than ten times as sensitive. The detectors respond in proportion to the strength, or amplitude, of a gravitational wave. Better strain sensitivity lets them pick up weaker waves, including those from more distant sources. For nearby sources, the volume of space they can search grows as the cube of strain sensitivity. In other words, doubling sensitivity increases the volume eightfold. For binary black holes with masses similar to GW150914, these observations surveyed about ten times the space-time volume of earlier searches. Space-time volume takes account of both the region within reach and the time spent observing it.

The two tools pick up waves that stretch space. But their data also have bursts of noise. These bursts can come from parts of the tools. The bursts can make it harder to see the waves. We can spot many of them in other data. Those data do not pick up waves in space. These other data show us what parts of the tools are doing. If a burst leaves a sign there, we can use it to spot noise. The other data help us tell some bursts from waves. We take out those bursts from our data. Some bursts may not leave a clear sign. We also count the bursts left when we work out the noise. We still need to allow for noise that we cannot take out. We look for bursts that happen at the same time. We found no sign that noise bursts in the two tools were linked in time.

The detectors record brief bursts of noise in their strain data, which measure how gravitational waves stretch space. These bursts can come from several different parts of the instruments. Many leave clear signs in other data channels that are not sensitive to gravitational waves. Each channel records a different kind of information about the instrument. A clear match between a burst and such a sign can help us identify its source. These channels help us tell noise from the instruments apart from signals caused by waves. We remove the bursts that we can identify in this way from our analyses. Some bursts may still remain in the strain data, so we account for them when we estimate the background noise for each detector, as described below. The background estimate still allows for bursts that are not removed. We found no evidence that noise bursts from the instruments in the two detectors were linked in time.

The detector strain data contain bursts of noise that do not follow a Gaussian, or bell-shaped, pattern. These brief transients can arise from several parts of the instruments. Many have recognizable signatures in auxiliary data channels, which do not respond to gravitational waves; these channels help us identify noise caused by the instruments rather than by waves. Each auxiliary channel provides a separate record of instrument behavior. A clear signature can help distinguish an instrumental event from a wave signal. We remove the identified transients from our analyses. Some noise bursts may still be left in the strain data. We use two ways to look for waves. Both ways use a time shift. We take data from one of two tools and move its times. We do not move the tools. We just change the times in one set of data. We move them more than a wave needs to get from one tool to the other. Then we look for new matches. The tools can make noise on their own. Some of that noise may seem to match even when there is no wave at all. This helps us see how often noise can match by chance. A match on its own does not prove that a wave was there. That gives us a way to judge a match we find in the real data. A real wave can match noise too. That can make noise seem more common, so we are more careful about calling a match real.

Noise is not the same at all times or at all pitches. A pitch can be high or low. A sound can change its pitch over time, like a tune. Some noise is a small bump. Some is much bigger. So some kinds of signals are harder to find than others. We sort the noise and the signals we find into groups. We use when they occur and how their pitch changes to do this. We look for such changes in the data. Noise can look more like a signal in one group than in another. We then ask how rare each signal is among the noise in its group. That way, we do not use the same yardstick for all the groups. This helps us find signals and judge them fairly. We take each group’s noise into account. Since we check more than one group, we lower how sure we are by the number of groups.

Noise changes across times and frequencies, or pitches. A frequency tells us how fast a signal changes. This means that some signals stand out more than others. For example, a pattern that is rare at one pitch may be more common at another. Some noise patterns can look more like a real event than other noise patterns do. We need to know what noise can look like before we can judge an event. To find signals more easily, we sort possible events and estimates of noise into groups. We use their patterns in time and frequency to do this. Then we compare each event with the noise in its own group. Each group gives us a fitting comparison for its events. This tells us how strong the evidence is for that event. Since we searched several groups, we reduce its significance by a factor equal to the number of groups.

Noise behaves differently at different times and frequencies. As a result, the background is not the same for every kind of signal. The background describes events that noise alone could produce. Some of these events may look like signals, so we need a way to tell how unusual a possible signal is. We then judge each event against the background in its own class. Each comparison uses the appropriate noise background. This gives us a better measure of how significant the event is. Because we searched several classes, we reduce that significance by a factor equal to the number of classes. Non-Gaussian noise does not follow a bell curve, and it varies across time and frequency. As a result, the background is not the same for all types of signals. This variation matters because a candidate’s apparent rarity depends on what kinds of noise it is compared with. To boost sensitivity and better judge events, we sort both background estimates and candidate events into classes based on their patterns in time and frequency. This search uses no specific waveform model. It identifies coincident excess power in time-frequency maps of detector strain data. These maps represent how the power in the data is distributed across frequency and time. It covers signal frequencies up to 1 kHz and durations up to a few seconds. A multidetector maximum likelihood method reconstructs waveforms consistent with a common gravitational-wave signal in both detectors. Each event is ranked by $\eta_c = \sqrt{2E_c/(1 + E_n/E_c)}$. Here $E_c$ is the dimensionless coherent signal energy, obtained by cross-correlating the two reconstructed waveforms. $E_n$ is the dimensionless residual noise energy after the reconstructed signal is subtracted from the data. The statistic measures the event’s signal-to-noise ratio and the agreement between the two detectors, combining signal strength with a penalty for residual noise. For a fixed coherent energy, a larger residual lowers the statistic. The ranking therefore favors events with both substantial shared energy and a reconstruction that leaves relatively little unexplained noise.

We search for gravitational waves from binaries with individual masses of 1 to 99 $M_\odot$, total mass below 100 $M_\odot$, and dimensionless spins up to 0.99. The spin parameter is dimensionless, and the mass bounds apply to the individual components and their sum. For systems above 4 $M_\odot$, we use an effective-one-body model. It combines post-Newtonian results, black hole perturbation theory, and numerical relativity. These approaches describe the dynamics and gravitational-wave emission of the binary; their combination provides a model for waveforms across the relevant mass range. The model assumes spins aligned with orbital angular momentum. Its templates can nevertheless recover systems with misaligned spins near GW150914’s parameters. We use approximately 250,000 template waveforms to cover the parameter space. Each template represents a modeled signal for a particular set of binary parameters. A large bank of templates enables the search to span the selected parameter space. We compare these templates with detector data to identify matching signals.

We look for waves by matching data from each detector to patterns. Each detector is a tool that can sense a wave. A pattern is a shape we expect a wave to make. Noise can make the data look like a wave, too. We find when each match is strongest. We check parts of the data to see if they fit the pattern. We do not just look at one part. We use a score to show how well the data fit. A good fit gets a high score. If not, we give the match a lower score. Next, we look for matches in both detectors. They must use the same pattern and be close in time. The two tools may see the wave at a bit different times. We use both scores to rank what we find. This helps us see which events give the best match. Then we can look at the pairs with the best scores.

We search for waves by comparing data from each detector with expected patterns. A detector is a tool that picks up signals. A pattern shows what a wave might look like in the data. We find when each pattern matches the data most strongly. A strong match gives a high score, but noise can also cause a match. Then we check the match in different parts of the signal. This extra check helps us see whether the signal fits the pattern as a whole, not just in one part. If the parts do not fit, we lower the score. We pair events seen in both detectors if they match the same pattern and arrive within 15 milliseconds of each other. The time limit lets a wave travel from one detector to the other and allows for small errors in its arrival time. Finally, we combine their scores to rank the paired events. The best scores point us toward the strongest matches in both detectors.

We compare data from each detector with predicted wave patterns, called templates, and find the strongest matches. Each template represents a waveform the search expects a merger to produce. A strong match alone does not guarantee that the data have the expected shape. For each match, we check whether different frequency bands, or ranges of signal frequency, fit the template. The extra test checks that the match is consistent across the signal, rather than concentrated in just one frequency range. If the fit is poor, we reduce the match’s score. We then pair events from the two detectors when they match the same template and arrive within 15 milliseconds of each other. The time window allows for the wave to travel between sites, as well as uncertainty in the arrival time of a weak signal. A paired event must satisfy both conditions. Finally, we combine the adjusted scores from both detectors to rank the paired events.

We search each detector’s data by matching it against predicted waveforms, or templates, and finding peaks in signal-to-noise ratio. The templates describe signals expected from merging compact objects. A peak marks an arrival time at which the template fits particularly well. For each peak, we test whether the data match the template across different frequency bands, reducing the score when the fit is poor. The test across bands helps distinguish a consistent signal from a match driven by noise in just one part of the data. We then select pairs of events from both detectors that match the same template and arrive within 15 milliseconds of each other. The 15-millisecond window accounts for travel time between the detector sites and uncertainty in the arrival time of weak signals. This coincidence requirement helps the search focus on events that could be seen at both sites. Finally, we rank these coincident events using the combined adjusted scores from the two detectors.

For each template in each detector, we calculate the matched-filter signal-to-noise ratio $\rho(t)$ and find its maxima over possible signal arrival times. At each maximum, we calculate a chi-squared statistic $\chi^2_r$ to test whether data in several frequency bands are consistent with the template. A value of $\chi^2_r$ near one indicates consistency with a coalescence, while a value above one leads us to reweight $\rho(t)$ as $\hat{\rho} = \rho/\{[1 + (\chi^2_r)^3]/2\}^{1/6}$. This reduces the score of a match that fits poorly across the frequency bands, rather than treating all strong matches as equally reliable. We then select coincident event pairs from the two detectors that match the same template and occur within 15 ms. This window allows 10 ms for propagation between sites and 5 ms for uncertainty in the arrival time of weak signals. Finally, we rank the coincident pairs by the quadrature sum $\hat{\rho}_c$ of the reweighted ratios $\hat{\rho}$ from both detectors.

A value near one suggests the data fit a merger signal. Values above one indicate a poorer fit and lead us to reduce the ranking score for that match. We select coincident events from the same template within 15 ms, allowing 10 ms for propagation between sites and 5 ms for arrival-time uncertainty. We rank these pairs by the quadrature sum $\hat{\rho}_c$ of their reweighted signal-to-noise ratios.

To find out what noise can do, we change the times of the peaks from one of our two tools. A peak is a high point in the data. We then look for peaks that line up in time with peaks from the other tool. We do this about ten million times. This gives us a way to test noise as if we had watched for 608,000 years. We use the test to see what might line up by chance. The tools can pick up noise as well as a signal. Some peaks may line up just by chance. We check for those chance matches again and again. For each test, we change the times in the data, not the tools. Then we look for new matches. Each set of matches helps us see what noise can do on its own. We do not have to wait 608,000 years to do these tests.

To learn what random noise can produce, we shift the times of peaks in one detector. A peak is a high point in the detector’s data. We then look for new matches between peaks in the two detectors. We repeat this process about ten million times to see which matches might happen by chance. Together, these tests give us the equivalent of 608,000 years of noise analysis. That does not mean the detectors ran for that long. The shifts change how the peaks from one detector line up with those from the other. This lets us build a sample of matches that random noise could create, even without a shared signal. The shifts change the recorded times for the test, not the detectors themselves. Each time we make a shift, we check the data for matches again. The full set of matches helps us see what noise alone could produce in this search.

To estimate the background from noise, we shift the times of signal-to-noise ratio peaks in one detector. These peaks mark strong responses in the search data. We then calculate a new set of coincident events: events that match in time across the two detectors. We repeat this procedure about ten million times to build a sample of events that noise could cause by chance. In total, the shifts give us the equivalent of 608,000 years of noise analysis, not 608,000 years of actual detector use. Each shift changes the relative timing of peaks between the detectors. By comparing events with this noise sample, we can judge whether a match is unusual for the background. The shifts change the times used in the test, not the detectors themselves. Each new comparison adds possible noise matches to the sample. Together, these repeated comparisons provide a much larger sample than a single check of the original detector times.

These events meet the search’s matching requirements using the shifted times instead of the original times. By repeating this procedure $\sim 10^7$ times, we build a background against which to assess events that might arise from noise. The resulting analysis is equivalent to 608,000 years of noise data, not 608,000 years of detector operation. Each shift changes the relative timing of peaks in the two detectors. We use the resulting sample to gauge how often noise alone can produce matching events. These repeated comparisons change the timing used in the calculation, not the detectors or the length of time they collected data. The many shifted searches provide a much larger sample of possible noise matches than a single comparison of the original times.

Repeating this procedure $\sim 10^7$ times produces a noise background analysis time equivalent to 608,000 years, with the accumulated duration representing repeated analyses rather than a single observing interval. Each shift changes the relative times of detector peaks, producing a sample of events that could arise from noise rather than a signal common to both detectors.

Noise can look like a wave. But noise is not the same for every wave shape. A wave shape is a kind of pattern. Some kinds of noise may look more like one pattern than another. The team sorted possible waves and noise into three groups. The groups were based on how long the wave shapes were. Shapes of much the same length went in the same group. The team looked at the noise in each group on its own. This helped them see how much a wave stood out from the noise in its group. They could then check a wave against the right group of noise. GW150914 stood out more than all the noise in its group. For all three groups, a false alarm this strong would be expected no more than once in 203,000 years. A second test found the same wave. It also backed up how sure the team was.

Background noise varies across the range of signals the search is designed to find. A second, independent search found the same signal with identical parameters and a consistent estimate of its significance.

We did it for GW150914, a wave made by two black holes. We make the noise test again after we take it out. A real wave should not be part of the noise we use for the next test. When we are sure that an event is a real gravitational wave, we remove it from the background used to test other events. The background shows what our tools might pick up by chance, rather than from a real wave. Some noise can look like a signal, so we need to know how often it might fool us. We did this for GW150914, a wave from two black holes joining. We make a new background after removing it. That way, the known wave is not counted as noise in the test. A purple line in the figure shows the result. We use it to check the other events. The next most significant event had a false alarm rate of one per 2.3 years. Its false alarm chance was 2 percent. This result does not tell us for sure whether the event was real or just noise. If real, it too may have come from two black holes joining.

When we identify a gravitational-wave signal with confidence, we remove it from the background used to assess other events. The background describes signals that noise could produce by chance. Some noise can resemble a real signal, so we use the background to judge how surprising each event is. We did this for GW150914, which came from two merging black holes. We make a fresh estimate after taking out the known signal. This keeps a confirmed wave from being counted as part of the noise used to assess the other events. A purple line in the figure shows the resulting background for the remaining events. The next most significant event had a false alarm rate of one per 2.3 years. Its false alarm probability was 0.02, or 2 percent. These figures do not establish whether the event was real. Its waveform, or signal shape, suggests that, if the event came from space rather than noise, it too was a black hole merger.

We look for waves in space. But our search gives us just a rough idea of what made them. These waves come from two black holes. A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that even light cannot get out. To learn more, we use ideas about how space and gravity work. Some show how the spin of a black hole can wobble. We use these ideas to find how big the holes are, how they spin, and how far away they are. The two holes join to make one new hole. We also work out how big that new hole is and how fast it spins. The larger hole did not spin as fast as it could. We know less about the smaller hole’s spin. Our answers are not exact. Our models help us see what the waves can tell us. They do not give us a perfect answer.

Our search is designed to find waves in space. But it gives only rough estimates of their source. The waves carry clues about the objects that made them. The models help us use those clues, rather than relying on the search alone. To get better estimates, we use models based on Einstein’s theory of gravity. Some models account for changes in the direction of a black hole’s spin. We estimate the holes’ masses and spins and their distance from us. The two black holes merge to form one new black hole. We also estimate the mass and spin of that final black hole. We report ranges, not exact values. The larger hole’s spin is below its maximum. The smaller hole’s spin is less certain. Our estimates also include errors from the data and the models. Different models can give somewhat different answers. We take those differences into account when we report how uncertain the results are.

General relativity is Einstein’s theory of gravity. It predicts the changing phase, or timing, of gravitational waves as two black holes spiral toward each other. As the black holes get closer, the waves change more quickly. We can express that phase as a sum of terms, each with a number set by the theory. These terms describe how the timing depends on the wave’s frequency, or how often it repeats. As the frequency rises, the signal changes. To test the theory, we change those numbers and check whether the resulting wave still matches our data. This puts limits on how much the numbers could differ from the predictions. We found no evidence that general relativity was violated.

Our observations constrain the rate at which stellar-mass binary black holes merge in the local universe. These systems consist of two black holes with masses comparable to those of stars.
